prompt.context: Your client is Galactica, a market leader in on-premise data warehousing and analytics technology. It makes money by selling hardware and software to large companies, as well as assisting them with tracking, storing, and analyzing their data. Galactica has a decentralized organizational structure and has offices in 40 countries, each run independently without much interference from corporate. Over the past several years Galactica's growth and profitability has declined due to large cloud providers, such as Amazon and Microsoft, taking a chunk of the market through their massive scale and resources. Last year, for the first time in its history, Galactica showed an annual loss.
prompt.question: We have been hired to find ways to cut costs while not sacrificing profitability. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.a: Roughly $3B of revenue last year; the company is publicly traded and based in the US but has clients globally.

clarifying_info.q: Does Galactica have a cloud offering?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, but it is small and cannot match the cost and services of the cloud market leaders. It does not believe it will be able to change this in the near term.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape for on-premise data warehousing?
clarifying_info.a: The on-premise market has had flat growth the last three years and is not expected to grow significantly going forward. Galactica competes primarily with IBM and Oracle in the on-premise space.

clarifying_info.q: What does decentralized structure mean in practice?
clarifying_info.a: Each country has near full autonomy on how operations are run and employs a full support staff of back-office functions. R&D spend and executive compensation takes place at the corporate level and is allocated proportionately to each country.

clarifying_info.q: Are we also looking at growth strategies?
clarifying_info.a: No. We have been hired solely to focus on cost cutting. Galactica is working on growth strategies internally.

exhibits.title: Country Performance Overview
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four country offices (Austria, Japan, Egypt, Germany) across four dimensions: 2015 revenue (USD millions), market size (USD millions), sales staff utilization percentage, and market position (rank).

data.footnote: Sales staff utilization % refers to how occupied the sales team was in 2015. 100% means they could not take any more leads; 0% means they had no leads to work on.

exhibits.title: Cost Data by Country
exhibits.shows: Cost data shared by interviewer only after the candidate asks: COGS by country and a uniform SG&A figure.

data.note: SG&A includes all other costs associated with running the office including depreciation and all allocated corporate overhead.

framework: Define cost structure: segment costs into COGS (hardware/software, delivery) and operating expenses (SG&A, R&D allocation, corporate overhead allocation)
Analyze by geography: assess each country office on revenue, cost, margin, market position, and growth potential to identify underperforming markets

Identify cost-reduction levers: office consolidation/exits, shared-service centralization of back-office functions, headcount optimization (sales utilization), procurement/vendor rationalization, R&D prioritization
Evaluate exit criteria: profitability, market size/share, strategic importance, feasibility of client transfer to another office
Quantify savings and risks for recommended actions; assess non-financial factors (talent, morale, regulatory, political)

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1 qualitatively. What does it tell you about each country office?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates interpret each country along multiple dimensions and identify implications for a cost-cutting mandate. Key conclusions: Austria — market leader but already serves 80% of a small market ($80M/$100M); limited upside; clients could potentially be served from Germany. Japan — largest market shown ($1.2B); not the leader but 100% sales utilization signals active growth potential; looks strong. Egypt — smallest revenue ($50M), lowest utilization (30%), 3rd market position; low traction in a mid-sized market; concern about ability to grow. Germany — largest revenue ($350M), 1st position, 90% utilization; highest potential. The key insight the candidate should flag: this is a cost case but the exhibit contains no cost data — they should ask for cost information by country.

questions.prompt: Given COGS by country (Austria $45M, Japan $70M, Egypt $30M, Germany $195M), SG&A of $30M for all countries, and a 40% tax rate, calculate profit by country.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a P&L waterfall for each country. The immediate takeaway is that Egypt is loss-making and Austria is marginally profitable. Strong candidates note Egypt should be exited and consider Austria as well. Candidate may calculate Egypt tax as $0 (loss) or as -$4M (tax benefit); $0 is the expected answer but -$4M is acceptable. Germany and Japan are clearly profitable and should be retained.

math.setup: For each country: Profit = (Revenue - COGS - SG&A) * (1 - Tax rate). Tax applies only if EBIT > 0; for Egypt EBIT is negative so tax = 0 (or candidate may use tax shield of $4M).
steps: Austria: Revenue $80M - COGS $45M = Gross $35M; $35M - SG&A $30M = EBIT $5M; Tax $5M*40% = $2M; Profit = $3M
Japan: Revenue $200M - COGS $70M = Gross $130M; $130M - SG&A $30M = EBIT $100M; Tax $100M*40% = $40M; Profit = $60M
Egypt: Revenue $50M - COGS $30M = Gross $20M; $20M - SG&A $30M = EBIT -$10M; Tax = $0 (loss); Profit = -$10M
Germany: Revenue $350M - COGS $195M = Gross $155M; $155M - SG&A $30M = EBIT $125M; Tax $125M*40% = $50M; Profit = $75M
math.answer: Austria: $3M profit | Japan: $60M profit | Egypt: -$10M loss | Germany: $75M profit. Total profit = $128M across four countries.

questions.prompt: Based on the financial analysis, which country or countries should Galactica consider exiting, and why?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately flag Egypt (loss-making, low utilization, 3rd place, limited growth prospects). Great candidates also flag Austria: barely profitable ($3M), small market already near-saturated (80% share), low incremental upside, and Germany could absorb Austrian clients given geographic proximity and shared German language, while Germany's 90% utilization means it could use the freed-up sales resources.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors should Galactica consider when exiting a country? How can they mitigate any risks associated with these factors?

categories.name: People & Talent
ideas: Loss of key talent (employees may leave or be difficult to relocate)
Mitigation: proactively identify top performers and offer transfer or retention packages to Germany or other offices

categories.name: Organizational & Political
ideas: Political difficulty of closing offices that have been run independently — especially Austria which is currently profitable and may resist the decision
Decentralized structure means local management may fight corporate directives
Mitigation: build a compelling financial model showing the rationale; involve local leadership early; create a joint transition steering committee

categories.name: Market Signaling
ideas: Exit signals weakness to the broader market and to existing customers in other regions
Customers may question Galactica's commitment and switch to competitors
Mitigation: craft a proactive communications strategy emphasizing focus and operational strength; offer client transition support

categories.name: Operational Continuity
ideas: Service disruption to existing clients in exiting markets
Increased corporate overhead allocated to remaining offices if fixed costs do not decrease proportionately
Mitigation: confirm Germany can absorb Austrian clients before closing; negotiate client transition timelines; verify fixed overhead is truly variable or avoidable

categories.name: Morale & Culture
ideas: Layoffs damage company morale across all offices, not just the closing ones
Remaining employees may worry about further closures
Mitigation: clear communication from CEO explaining the strategic rationale; show investment in remaining markets

recommendation: Good: Galactica should exit Egypt. It is losing $10M per year, holds only the 3rd market position, and has 30% sales utilization — indicating the team is struggling to find opportunities. The savings from SG&A elimination ($30M) will meaningfully improve profitability.

Great: Galactica should exit both Egypt and Austria. Egypt is straightforwardly loss-making. Austria is marginally profitable ($3M) with a near-saturated small market and limited upside. Closing the Austrian office and transitioning its clients to Germany is feasible given geographic proximity and a shared language, and frees up SG&A and sales capacity that Germany (90% utilized and #1 in a large market) can redeploy to accelerate growth.
risks: Exiting Egypt and Austria creates political friction given the decentralized, independently-run structure — especially Austria which is currently profitable
Risk of losing key talent in both markets
Negative market signal that could prompt other clients globally to question Galactica's commitment
Potential SG&A increase for remaining offices if some corporate overhead is fixed and reallocated
next_steps: Build a detailed financial model quantifying cost savings and transition costs (severance, lease terminations) for exiting Egypt and Austria
Confirm that Germany can operationally serve existing Austrian clients — assess language, time-zone, and capacity
Develop a communications plan for internal stakeholders (employees) and external stakeholders (clients, market) to manage perception
Engage local leadership in Egypt and Austria early to identify key talent and begin retention/transfer discussions
